convolution.title: Convolution: the moving overlap
convolution.subtitle: A rectangle convolved with a decaying exponential. Move t and watch the overlap area become y(t).

controls.title: Parameters
controls.description: x(t) is a unit rectangle on [-0.5, 0.5]; h(t) = e^'{'-t'}'u(t).
controls.timeHint: Move the reversed kernel across the input.

plot.overlapDescription: The shaded region is the integrand; its area is the output at this t.
plot.outputDescription: The marker follows the area under the product as t moves.

steps.title: Four operations
steps.shift: Shift by t to obtain h(t−τ).

observe.title: What to notice
observe.noOverlap: Before t = −0.5 the signals never overlap, so the output stays zero.
observe.rising: Between −0.5 and 0.5 the overlap grows: the output rises like 1 − e^'{'−(t+0.5)'}'.
observe.falling: After 0.5 the overlap shrinks and the output decays exponentially.
observe.area: Convolution is not pointwise multiplication; it accumulates area over the whole overlap.

sampling.title: Sampling and aliasing
sampling.subtitle: Sample a cosine at different rates. Below the Nyquist rate, a fast signal leaves a slow-looking set of samples.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.description: x(t) = cos(2π f₀ t), sampled every T_s = 1/f_s seconds.
controls.signalHint: The physical frequency you want to capture.
controls.samplingHint: The number of samples taken per second.

readouts.aliasHint: The low-frequency cosine that fits the same samples.

plot.title: Continuous signal, samples and alias
plot.description: Dots are the samples the system actually sees. The dashed curve is an alias that passes through the same dots.

theory.title: Why aliasing happens
theory.nyquist: A real sinusoid is uniquely determined by samples only when f_s > 2f₀. The threshold 2f₀ is the Nyquist rate.
theory.overlap: Sampling multiplies by an impulse train, which copies the spectrum every f_s. When copies overlap, high frequencies fold down.
theory.edge: At exactly f_s = 2f₀ the samples determine the frequency but not the phase, so this is a boundary case rather than a comfortable design point.

experiment.title: Try this
experiment.lowRate: Set f_s to 6 Hz with f₀ = 5 Hz. Predict the apparent frequency before looking at the readout.
experiment.increase: Raise f_s above 10 Hz and watch the alias disappear.
experiment.compare: Compare the number of samples per period with the visual smoothness of the reconstruction.
experiment.question: If the samples alone are given, can you tell 5 Hz from 7 Hz at f_s = 12 Hz?

fourierSeries.title: Fourier series: from sine waves to a square wave
fourierSeries.subtitle: A square wave is an infinite sum of odd harmonics. Increase N and watch the edges sharpen while the ripple stays.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.description: The fundamental is 1 Hz. Only odd harmonics contribute.
controls.harmonicsHint: N is always odd; the slider adds two harmonics at a time.

readouts.overshootHint: Above the ideal square-wave level of 1

plot.timeDescription: The dashed line is the ideal square wave; the solid line is the finite partial sum.

insight.title: What the spectrum tells you
insight.odd: The square wave has odd symmetry, so only sine terms with odd k survive.
insight.decay: Harmonic amplitude falls as 1/k: high frequencies are present, but progressively weaker.
insight.gibbs: Near a jump the partial sum overshoots by about 9% and the overshoot does not vanish as N grows.
insight.convergence: More harmonics reduce the transition width, so the approximation converges in energy even though the pointwise error at the jump does not go away.

experiment.title: Try this
experiment.step: Set N = 1 and notice that the result is just a sine wave.
experiment.observe: Increase N to 31 and watch the edge get steeper while the ripple remains.
experiment.spectrum: Predict the amplitude of the 9th harmonic before checking the spectrum.

firstOrder.title: First-order systems: the time constant
firstOrder.subtitle: A first-order step response reaches 63.2% at one time constant, 95% at three, and is essentially settled at five.

controls.title: Parameters
controls.description: K is the DC gain and τ sets how fast the system responds.
controls.gainHint: The final value of the step response.
controls.timeConstantHint: Larger τ means a slower system.

readouts.settlingHint: Within about 1% of the final value

plot.title: Step response
plot.description: The horizontal dashed line is the final value K = {value}.

insight.title: Why 63.2%?
insight.definition: τ is the time for the response to cover 1 − e^'{'−1'}' ≈ 63.2% of the remaining distance to the final value.
insight.meaning: At t = τ the slope has already fallen to 1/e of its initial value, so the response visibly slows down.
insight.bandwidth: A slower time response means a narrower bandwidth: f_c = 1/(2πτ).
insight.gain: K scales the whole response vertically; it does not change the settling time.

experiment.title: Try this
experiment.changeTau: Double τ and observe that the 63.2% point moves to the right.
experiment.changeGain: Change K and confirm that the shape stays the same while the final value scales.
experiment.readPoint: Read y at τ, 2τ and 3τ, then compare with the readouts.
experiment.connect: Connect the cutoff frequency to the time constant: smaller τ means wider bandwidth.

tasks.L1-1: Build a time array and generate sine, step, exponential and triangular signals. Write your own cosine and rectangle expressions. Compare shifts, reversal, compression and combined transforms; verify their effects on peak time, height and support width, and use midpoint sums to check h=S/Δ for fixed-area rectangular pulses.
tasks.L1-2: Test affine, timescale, delay, integrator and square systems for linearity and time invariance with causal inputs. Change inputs and coefficients to construct counterexamples; compare both paths and their difference, and record the parameters and limits of finite tests.
tasks.L1-3: Compute zero-input, zero-state and total responses. Change the initial state and input switch, read specified times and verify the sum of components.
tasks.L1-4: In the interactive experiment, compare 10/20 ms windows on 50 Hz interference and confirm that 20 ms covers one period. Then compare R-wave distortion and center delay with Python windows of 0.02/0.08 s, using t−W/2 for the data center, and halve dt to check integration error.
tasks.L2-1: Sum odd sine harmonics in a loop. Compare term counts, highest frequencies and overshoot for K=3, 7 and 15. Distinguish harmonic order from number of terms.
tasks.L2-2: Generate a rectangular pulse and approximate its continuous Fourier integral with an FFT. Compare the analytic spectrum while changing width, amplitude and delay. Check scaling and avoid phase readings at spectral zeros.
tasks.L2-3: Use both cutoff constraints to show that a first-order low-pass is infeasible; specify the notch center and alpha, then compare waveform distortion for narrow and wide notches.
tasks.L2-4: Compare low-frequency sampling and 3 kHz / 4 kHz audio aliasing. Use an independent Butterworth anti-alias low-pass at fixed playback gain; the 50 Hz ECG notch cannot replace this low-pass.
tasks.L3-1: Generate exponential, delayed-step and rectangular signals. Numerically integrate at several s points within a convergence region and compare with your own derivations. Extend the window to assess truncation.
tasks.L3-2: Solve the first-order equation for initial values 0, 0.5 and 2. Compare total, zero-input and zero-state responses, retain sY−y₀ in the derivation, measure y(1) and the zero-state t90, and record numerical error.
tasks.L3-3: Change center and alpha; compare zeros, poles, ECG response and frequency response. For alpha<0, distinguish the algebraic slice from a steady-state response.
tasks.L3-4: Generate pulses with different durations and solve each output in smooth segments. Add your own candidates near the threshold and record failures and successes. Justify the shortest duration using a derivation and parameter resolution.

ecg.title: Choose an averaging window for ECG
ecg.input: Before: the same noisy ECG segment
ecg.moveTime: Drag output time to move the shaded window
ecg.windowRule: Only data from the preceding {width} ms, shaded on the left, are averaged. The result is assigned to output time; the dashed vertical line marks the data center.
ecg.compareFirst: View both window widths and compare the output before answering.
ecg.moveFirst: Compare both widths, then drag output time by at least one step to observe the shaded window.
ecg.connection: The moving average you used is a convolution
ecg.convolution: Move a rectangular window of width W and unit area along the ECG. At each output time, average the data inside the window to obtain one point on the output plot.
ecg.takeaway: An ideal sinusoid cancels when the window spans an integer number of periods; for period P, the shortest full-cycle window is W=P. Both 20 ms and 80 ms cover whole cycles of the 50 Hz interference here. For a causal window [t−W,t], the data center is ((t−W)+t)/2=t−W/2, while the result is labeled at t. A wider window distorts the R wave more, so W/2 is the window's time-center difference, not an exact shift of every ECG peak.
ecg.operationInstruction: Open O1 and O2. Switch widths or drag time, then answer from the plots. Operations: 5 points; window selection, R-wave preservation, and sample timing: 15 points; two principle questions: 5 points.

noise.title: Inspect interference
noise.instruction: An averaging window takes the mean of the preceding W ms of data. Start with interference alone: the ripple repeats every 20 ms. View 10 ms and 20 ms windows and check whether the averaged ripple remains.
noise.question: How does the 20 ms output compare with the 10 ms output?

options.flat: It approaches zero; ripple remains at 10 ms

noise.feedback: 20 ms covers a full cycle. Positive and negative areas cancel, giving zero average for an ideal 50 Hz sine. 10 ms covers only half a cycle and generally leaves ripple. These plots show output after the window has filled. For another sinusoid, if its period is P, the shortest full-cycle window is W=P.

shape.title: Preserve the R wave
shape.instruction: Return to the full ECG. The dashed line is the clean reference; the tall spike near 400 ms is the R wave. Compare its height and width using 20 ms and 80 ms windows.
shape.question: Both windows cancel the ideal 50 Hz sine. Which keeps the R wave closer to the clean reference?

options.short: 20 ms preserves the R wave better
options.long: 80 ms: smoother always means more accurate
options.equal: Neither window affects the R wave

shape.feedback: 80 ms mixes more neighboring data: the R wave is lower and wider, and its timing changes. When both cancel the ideal 50 Hz sine, 20 ms causes less distortion to this ECG segment.

timing.title: Follow the window
timing.instruction: The shaded interval in the input plot contains the data being averaged. The solid vertical line in the output plot marks output time. Switch widths and drag time, then compare the window center with output time below.
timing.question: As the window moves, where is the center of the averaged data relative to output time?

options.before: Earlier: the result is output later

timing.feedback: Causal averaging uses past and current data. The center of [t−W,t] is ((t−W)+t)/2=t−W/2: 10 ms earlier for a 20 ms window and 40 ms earlier for an 80 ms window. This explains the greater linear-phase delay of the wider window. ECG peaks also distort, so their shifts need not equal W/2.

responseDiagnosis.scoring: Assessment: 25 points. Operations: 5; diagnosis, test selection and prediction: 5 each; principles: 5.
responseDiagnosis.originalChart: Outputs before and after the adjustment
responseDiagnosis.sourceQuestion: What changed, based on the two curves?
responseDiagnosis.testQuestion: Which test isolates the effect of the {target}?
responseDiagnosis.predictionQuestion: After correctly isolating the {target}, will the two curves overlap throughout?

tests.inputOff: Turn both inputs off; keep their respective initial states
tests.resetInitial: Reset both initial states to zero; keep their respective inputs
tests.clearBoth: Clear both inputs and both initial states
tests.repeat: Repeat both runs under their original conditions

predictions.different: Differ during part of the interval

responseDiagnosis.wrongTest: This operation does not isolate the requested source. Choose: {test}. Revise your choice to run verification.
responseDiagnosis.revealed: Adjusted case: initial value {initial}, step amplitude {amplitude}.
responseDiagnosis.principle: The starting value reflects the initial state; the limiting value reflects the sustained input. Turning the input off leaves the zero-input response; clearing the initial state leaves the zero-state response.

responseDiagnosis.saveFailed: Could not save the attempt. Try again.

blackBox.operationInstruction: Open a checkpoint, compare both probes of the same black box, then submit the output height or timing and your judgment.
blackBox.compareFirst: View and compare both probes before entering readings and judgments.
blackBox.title: Identify the black boxes
blackBox.mission: Send test pulses to each unknown device and choose the one rule that explains all its outputs. Each device has three candidates; the candidates and their order vary, and a rule may appear again. Judge each device from its own input and output.
blackBox.sendStep: 1 · Send pulses and observe the output
blackBox.probeRule: Each test starts from the same baseline: height 1, starting at 1 s, lasting 1 s. Double amplitude changes only the height; Send 1 s later changes only the start. Every test is recorded automatically.
blackBox.conclusion: Identification results for all three boxes
blackBox.identifyStep: 2 · Select this box's observations, then identify its model
blackBox.heightQuestion: When the input height changes from 1 to 2, what is the output height?
blackBox.shiftQuestion: When the input is sent 1 second later, how far does the output move from the baseline?
blackBox.chooseEvidence: Choose from this box's test records
blackBox.retryHeight: The height does not match this box's record. Check the output height in the doubled-amplitude row and choose again.
blackBox.retryShift: The time shift does not match this box's records. Subtract the baseline output start from the delayed test's output start and choose again.
blackBox.reasoningRecord: Observation evidence: when input height changes from 1 to 2, output height is {height}; sending the input 1 s later shifts the output by {shift} s.
blackBox.plot: Dashed: input; solid: device output · Time / s, amplitude

observations.baseline: Baseline: input height {inputHeight}, starting at {inputStart} s for 1 s; output height {outputHeight}, starting at {outputStart} s for {outputWidth} s.
observations.double: Change amplitude only: the input doubles from 1 to {inputHeight}, and the output becomes {outputHeight}. Compare the curve heights and the baseline row.
observations.shift: Change timing only: the input starts at {inputStart} s instead of 1 s, and the output starts at {outputStart} s. Relative to the baseline, did the output also move by exactly 1 s?

blackBox.start: Select “Send baseline pulse” above to start testing this box.
blackBox.needTests: Send the baseline, then double its amplitude and send it 1 second later. Once all three rows are recorded, select this box's two observations and its model.

models.timescale: Compress time by a factor of two
models.stretch: Stretch time by a factor of two

choiceFeedback.square: This candidate maps input height 1 to output 1, and input height 2 to output 4. Check this device's baseline and doubled-amplitude records.
choiceFeedback.delay: This candidate always starts the output 1 s after the input, keeping the height and width. Check this device's start times and pulse widths.
choiceFeedback.timescale: This candidate halves both the start time and width. Check the baseline start, output width and delayed-input record for this device.
choiceFeedback.gain: This candidate maps baseline input height 1 to output 2, and doubled input height 2 to output 4. Check both output heights for this device.
choiceFeedback.attenuate: This candidate maps input height 1 to output 0.5, and input height 2 to output 1. Check this device's height records.
choiceFeedback.identity: This candidate keeps the input height, start time and width unchanged in every test. Compare this device's input and output across all three tests.
choiceFeedback.offset: This candidate maps input height 1 to output 2 and input height 2 to output 3; the output is also 1 wherever the input is zero. Check the graph and height records.
choiceFeedback.invert: This candidate turns a positive input pulse into a negative output pulse. Check whether this device's output is above or below zero.
choiceFeedback.delayTwo: This candidate starts the output 2 s after the input. Subtract the baseline input start from the output start to check the gap.
choiceFeedback.advance: This candidate starts the output 1 s before the input. An input starting at 1 s should produce an output starting at 0 s. Check this device's start times.
choiceFeedback.stretch: This candidate makes the output 2 s wide. Delaying the input by 1 s moves the output by 2 s. Check the width and the two output start times.
choiceFeedback.cube: This candidate changes the output height from 1 to 8 when the input height changes from 1 to 2. Check this device's doubled-amplitude record.

retry.square: This model disagrees with the doubled-amplitude test. Compare the input and output heights and try again.
retry.delay: This model disagrees with the pulse position or width. Compare when the input and output start and how far apart they are.
retry.timescale: This model does not explain the output width and start time. Check how far the output moves when the input is sent 1 second later.

explanations.square: An input height of 1 gives 1; doubling it to 2 gives 4, rather than 2. The square operator is therefore nonlinear. It applies the same square operation at every time, so shifting the input shifts the output equally: it is time invariant.
explanations.delay: The output keeps the input height and width and always starts 1 second later. A delay preserves superposition, so it is linear. Sending the input 1 second later also delays the output by 1 second, so it is time invariant.
explanations.timescale: The output width is half the input width. Moving the input start from 1 to 2 s moves the output start from 0.5 to 1 s, a shift of only 0.5 s. The system is time varying. Time scaling still preserves superposition, so it is linear.

blackBox.principle: These tests distinguish the three candidate models in this task. A counterexample disproves a property; use the revealed formula to justify a positive conclusion. One amplitude-doubling test cannot prove linearity.
blackBox.linear: Linear: does the system preserve input superposition?
blackBox.invariant: Time invariant: does delaying the input only delay the output equally?
blackBox.analysisRecord: Box {id}: {model}; linear: {linear}; time invariant: {invariant}. Baseline, doubled-amplitude and 1-second-delayed input/output tests recorded.

L1-1.question: For 2f(2(t−1)), how do the peak time and height change?
L1-1.conclusion: Use the readings to verify the general transform y(t)=A f(a(t−t₀)): an original peak at t_p moves to t₀+t_p/a, its height is multiplied by A, and support width is divided by |a|. A fixed-area S rectangular pulse has height S/Δ.

steps.original: Original: read peak time and height
steps.shift: Set the shift to 1 s and compare the peak position
steps.reverse: Set scale a to −1 and observe reversal
steps.compress: Set scale a to 2 and observe compression
steps.pulse0: Set the pulse width to 0.5 s and read its height
steps.pulse1: Set the pulse width to 0.2 s and read its height
steps.pulse2: Set the pulse width to 0.1 s and read its height

L1-1.given: Original f(t): a triangular pulse from 0 to 3 s, with its peak at (1 s, 1).
L1-1.objective: Compare the original and combined transform, record peak time, height and support width, then use midpoint sums to check narrow-pulse height and area.
L1-1.pulseGiven: Reference pulse: Δ=0.5 s, height 2, area 1. The area stays 1 as the width changes.

L1-2.question: Predict whether each of the five systems is linear and time invariant. Add reasons after the comparisons.
L1-2.predictionGuide: For each system, enter “linear: yes/no; time invariant: yes/no.” These are initial guesses; no proof is needed yet.

x+1: linear __; time invariant __
x(2t): linear __; time invariant __
x(t−1): linear __; time invariant __
Integrator: linear __; time invariant __

L1-2.conclusion: Complete the linearity and time-invariance result for each system, with reasons. A nonzero difference is a counterexample; use the definitions to reason about properties not measured directly.
L1-2.conclusionGuide: Each system is directly tested for one property. Use the definitions above to determine its other property.

x(2t): linear __; time invariant __; reason __

Integrator: linear __; time invariant __; reason __

L1-2.linearityDescription: Combine the inputs with their coefficients before the system. The result should equal the weighted sum of the separate outputs.
L1-2.timeInvariantDescription: Shift the input before the system. The result should equal shifting the system output afterward.
L1-2.parameterRecordHelp: Nothing to fill in or copy. Select “Record and continue” to save the parameters shown here with this comparison.
L1-2.linearityRecord: Input x₁: {x1}; input x₂: {x2}; superposition coefficients α: {alpha}, β: {beta}
L1-2.timeShiftRecord: Input x: {x1}; time shift d: {delay} s
L1-2.linearityPathA: A · Combine inputs, then apply the system
L1-2.linearityPathB: B · Apply the system separately, then combine outputs
L1-2.timeShiftPathA: A · Shift the input, then apply the system
L1-2.timeShiftPathB: B · Apply the system, then shift its output
L1-2.action1: Read the system formula and the two operation paths A and B above. This step tests the property named in its heading.
L1-2.action2: Predict whether paths A and B will differ, then select “Show comparison.” Keep the presets; no parameter changes or numeric estimate are needed.
L1-2.action3: Compare the marked time on both plots and read the listed A, B and difference values. Select “Different” or “Same,” record the result and continue.
L1-2.parameterEffect: Changing x₁ or x₂ changes the input signals; α or β changes their weights; d changes the time shift. These edits change both outputs and the difference curve. Use the presets for the required comparisons. After an edit, estimate again and submit to see the new plots. The next comparison restores its preset.
L1-2.estimateGuide: Predict whether outputs A and B differ. No number is needed. The plots will mark the same time and list A, B and their difference.
L1-2.readoutTitle: Read both paths at one time
L1-2.readoutTime: Both plots mark t={time} s. The output values are listed below, so there is no need to copy numbers from the graph.
L1-2.outputPlotTitle: Outputs from paths A and B
L1-2.differencePlotGuide: Use this plot to see where the paths differ. Its marker matches the output plot; the exact values are listed below.
L1-2.differenceRule: One case where the paths differ is a counterexample: the system fails this property. If they match here, that only shows agreement for these inputs; one test cannot prove the general rule.

instructions.affine: Test linearity of x+1: compare combining the inputs before adding the constant with adding the constant to each output first.
instructions.square: Test linearity of x²: compare combining the inputs before squaring with squaring each input separately.
instructions.timescale: Test time invariance of x(2t): compare shifting the input before time compression with shifting the output afterward.
instructions.delay: Test time invariance of x(t−1): compare shifting the input before the system with shifting the system output afterward.
instructions.integrator: Test time invariance of the integrator: compare shifting the input before integration with shifting the integrated output afterward.

steps.linear1: x²: compare the two superposition paths
steps.shift1: x²: compare the two time-shift paths
steps.linear2: t·x: compare the two superposition paths
steps.shift2: t·x: compare the two time-shift paths

L1-2.given: Inputs in this experiment are zero for t<0.
L1-2.objective: Complete five preset comparisons: predict whether the paths differ, inspect A, B and their difference at one marked time, then record what you observe. Finally classify linearity and time invariance for all five systems.

L2-1.question: Will adding harmonics remove overshoot at a square-wave jump?
L2-1.conclusion: Compare K=3 and K=15. Where is the approximation better, and how does overshoot change?

L2-2.question: Does a narrower rectangular pulse have a wider or narrower spectrum?
L2-2.conclusion: What does width, time shift and amplitude each change in the spectrum? Use the first pair of zeros to relate main-lobe width to pulse width.

L2-2.objective: Verify how pulse width, delay and amplitude change the spectrum, and find the main-lobe width from the first pair of zeros.

L2-3.question: Can a first-order low-pass preserve the 10 Hz ECG component and suppress 50 Hz interference? If not, how can a notch filter help?
